Seventy percent had goals. Only 3% wrote them down.

Kevin Trudeau shares the story of a Harvard graduating class. Most students said they had specific goals for the next 10 to 20 years. When asked who had them on paper, only 3% raised a hand.

Fifteen years later, Kevin says, that small group had achieved more than the other 97% combined.

His point: a goal in your head is vague. A goal on paper is real.

Do you have your biggest goal written down right now?

Knowledge is only power if you can recall it.

Kevin Trudeau gets worked up about people who look everything up on a screen. He says that if you have to check your computer or phone for every answer, you are helpless.

But when the data sits at your mental fingertips, you have all your weapons ready. For Kevin, knowledge is power only if it is used, and it can only be used if it is remembered.

When did you last need an answer and have it ready in your head?

Sometimes the smartest move is getting mad.

Kevin Trudeau points to a famous Rocky fight scene. Rocky is covering up and taking a beating, and his corner is shouting at him to get out. Then someone says: he's getting mad.

Kevin says that was the magic of success. Anger moved Rocky to act, because he knew what he did not want. From there he could decide what he did want.

What is something you are no longer willing to put up with?

You can answer your address instantly. But what do you want?

Kevin Trudeau says he asks people their name, address and phone number, and they answer in a flash. Then he asks, what do you want? They have to think about it.

That, Kevin says, is the problem. Without a specific, measurable end result, you have no target. And you can't hit a target you don't have.

Could you say exactly what you want without pausing?

One small win can start a whole momentum cycle.

Kevin Trudeau says many people carry a poor picture of themselves, and it quietly limits the life they build.

He explains that even a small change brings small wins: a raise, a new relationship, a lucky meeting. Then a cycle starts. Success builds confidence, confidence creates activity, activity creates success habits, and those create more success.

What is one small win that could start your cycle?

#ad #confidence #success #habits

Arnold didn't just wish. He saw it every night.

Kevin Trudeau points to Arnold Schwarzenegger's documentary. As a young man in Austria, Arnold put a picture of what he wanted on the wall by his bed. Every night he closed his eyes and saw himself on stage winning, with the crowd cheering. He felt as if it was real.

Then, Kevin says, he got up early and went to work on the next logical step.

What would you picture every night if you knew you'd act on it?

Typing leaves less of a mark on your brain than writing.

Kevin Trudeau explains why he asks people to write their goals on paper. He says cursive writing fires thousands of neural pathways because of the many movements of your hand.

Typing, he says, uses fewer than two dozen movements, and thumbs on a phone use even fewer. So writing it by hand makes a far bigger impression in your brain.

When did you last write something by hand that mattered?
